First, for every integer \(1\le j\le S/h\), every (binary or fractional) vertex cover on \([-\gamma,\gamma]\cap\mathbb Z\) of all edges \((l,l+j)\) in this interval has total \(k_l\) weight at least \(M\), uniformly for large \(n\). To see this extend the weights to the untruncated Cauchy kernel \(h K_{\rm Cau}(lh-v_0^*)\), \(K_{\rm Cau}(x)=1/[\pi(1+x^2)]\), and extend the cover by weight 1 at all vertices outside the interval (cost \(<.0001\) for large \(n\), by e.g. the tail bound and \(O(h)\) Riemann error). A fractional cover means vertex numbers in \([0,1]\) with endpoint sums \(\ge1\); on each residue chain mod \(j\) these can be rounded to a random binary cover preserving expected weight (select where the vertex number is at least its threshold), by a uniform threshold \(U_0\in[0,1]\) at even vertices (center counted as even in each chain) and threshold \(1-U_0\) at odd vertices (use non-strict comparison). In each chain take a central vertex \(l\) nearest to \(v_0^*/h\). All weights are nonincreasing outward on each of its two arms. For binary covers the minimum weight is the lesser of the two alternating parity cover weights: if center is omitted, both first neighbors are forced, then pair disjoint edges at offsets \((2,3),(4,5),\ldots\) on each arm require at least the odd weights there; if center is included, edges \((1,2),(3,4),\ldots\) on each arm require the even weights. This reasoning works for the infinite chain by summability.
